prompt: What do Layer 2 discovery protocols do?
chosen: They let devices share information about themselves with their directly connected neighbours, so you can map out the network — identifying devices, their models, how they are connected, and their IP addresses.
rejected: They discover the shortest Layer 2 path between two devices and use it to forward frames more efficiently.

prompt: Why are Layer 2 discovery protocols useful?
chosen: Because network documentation is often out of date or was never done properly. These protocols let you build an accurate picture of the network from the devices themselves.
rejected: Because they automatically generate and update the network diagram files stored on each device.

prompt: What is CDP?
chosen: Cisco Discovery Protocol, a Cisco-proprietary Layer 2 discovery protocol that runs on Cisco routers and switches. It is enabled by default.
rejected: Cisco Discovery Protocol, an IEEE standard that any vendor may implement on their network devices.

prompt: Is CDP enabled by default?
chosen: Yes. Unless you want to change the default settings, no configuration is needed to use it.
rejected: No. Like LLDP, it must be enabled globally with the cdp run command before it will operate.

prompt: What multicast MAC address does CDP use?
chosen: 0100.0ccc.cccc.

prompt: Do switches flood CDP messages?
chosen: No. Even though they are multicast, a switch receives a CDP frame for itself rather than flooding it, and adds the sender to its own CDP neighbour table.
rejected: Yes. Like any multicast frame, CDP messages are flooded out all ports except the one they arrived on.

prompt: What does show cdp neighbors display?
chosen: A list of the device's CDP neighbours with basic details — device ID, local interface, holdtime, capability, platform, and port ID.
rejected: A list of all Cisco devices on the network, including those several hops away, along with their routing tables.

prompt: What does the Local Intrfce column mean?
chosen: The interface on the local device that the neighbour is connected to.
rejected: The interface on the neighbouring device that connects back to the local device.

prompt: What does the Port ID column mean?
chosen: The interface on the neighbouring device. This is the one people most often confuse with Local Intrfce, which is the local device's own port.
rejected: The Layer 4 port number that CDP uses to exchange its advertisements.

prompt: What does the Holdtme column show?
chosen: How many seconds remain before the local device removes that neighbour's entry. It resets to the full holdtime each time an advertisement arrives.
rejected: How many seconds the neighbour has been in the CDP neighbour table since it was first discovered.

prompt: What does the Capability column indicate?
chosen: The type of device — R for router, S for switch, and so on. A device can show several codes if it has multiple capabilities.
rejected: Which CDP features the neighbouring device supports, such as version 2 advertisements.

prompt: What does the Platform column show?
chosen: The hardware model of the neighbouring device.
rejected: The operating system version running on the neighbouring device.

prompt: What does show cdp neighbors detail add?
chosen: Much more information than the summary view, including the neighbour's full software version, VTP domain, native VLAN, and duplex setting.
rejected: The same information as show cdp neighbors, but formatted vertically for easier reading on narrow terminals.

prompt: What does show cdp entry do?
chosen: It shows the same detail as show cdp neighbors detail, but for only the neighbour you name. Useful when a device has many neighbours.
rejected: It shows a single line of summary information for the neighbour you name, without the detail.

prompt: What command confirms whether CDP is enabled?
chosen: show cdp. If it is enabled you see the timers and version; if not, you get a message saying CDP is not enabled.
rejected: show cdp status, which prints either ACTIVE or INACTIVE.

prompt: What is the default CDP advertisement timer?
chosen: 60 seconds.
rejected: 30 seconds, the same as LLDP.

prompt: What is the default CDP holdtime?
chosen: 180 seconds — three minutes.
rejected: 120 seconds — two minutes.

prompt: What does the CDP holdtime actually tell the neighbour?
chosen: How long to keep this device in its neighbour table after it stops receiving advertisements. The device is telling its neighbour how long to wait before removing it.
rejected: How long this device will keep the neighbour in its own table before removing it.

prompt: What command changes the CDP advertisement timer?
chosen: cdp timer, followed by the number of seconds, in global configuration mode.
rejected: cdp advertise, followed by the number of seconds, in interface configuration mode.

prompt: What command changes the CDP holdtime?
chosen: cdp holdtime, followed by the number of seconds, in global configuration mode.
rejected: cdp hold, followed by the number of seconds, in interface configuration mode.

prompt: Which CDP version is sent by default?
chosen: Version 2. You can fall back to version 1 with no cdp advertise-v2, which is only needed for very old neighbouring devices.
rejected: Version 1, for maximum compatibility. Version 2 must be enabled explicitly with cdp advertise-v2.

prompt: How do you disable CDP on the whole device?
chosen: no cdp run, in global configuration mode. Use cdp run to turn it back on.
rejected: no cdp enable, in global configuration mode.

prompt: How do you disable CDP on one interface?
chosen: no cdp enable, in interface configuration mode. That interface then neither sends CDP advertisements nor processes ones it receives.
rejected: no cdp run, in interface configuration mode.

prompt: If CDP is disabled globally, does cdp enable on an interface do anything?
chosen: No. With CDP disabled globally, it won't be active on any interface regardless of the per-interface setting.
rejected: Yes. The interface-level command overrides the global setting, so CDP runs on that one interface.

prompt: Why might you want to disable CDP?
chosen: Security. CDP reveals a lot about the device, including its software version, which an attacker could use to look up known vulnerabilities and launch a targeted attack.
rejected: Performance. CDP advertisements consume significant bandwidth on busy links, which can slow down user traffic.

prompt: What does show cdp interface display?
chosen: The CDP status of interfaces, including the encapsulation and the CDP timers. If CDP is disabled on an interface it says so.
rejected: A list of which neighbours are connected to each interface, with their hardware models.

prompt: What does show cdp traffic display?
chosen: Statistics on how many CDP messages the device has sent and received, broken down by version.
rejected: The bandwidth consumed by CDP messages as a percentage of total interface throughput.

prompt: What is LLDP?
chosen: Link Layer Discovery Protocol, the IEEE's vendor-neutral equivalent to CDP. It is defined in IEEE 802.1AB and any vendor can implement it.
rejected: Link Layer Discovery Protocol, Cisco's successor to CDP, which adds support for discovering devices more than one hop away.

prompt: What standard defines LLDP?
chosen: IEEE 802.1AB.
rejected: IEEE 802.1AX.

prompt: What multicast MAC address does LLDP use?
rejected: 0100.0ccc.cccc.

prompt: Is LLDP enabled by default on Cisco devices?
chosen: No. Cisco devices support it but it is disabled by default. You enable it globally with lldp run.
rejected: Yes. Both CDP and LLDP run by default on modern Cisco routers and switches.

prompt: When should you use LLDP instead of CDP?
chosen: When the network has devices from multiple vendors. If everything is Cisco, the default CDP is fine.
rejected: When the network is large, since LLDP scales to more neighbours than CDP can handle.

prompt: Can a device run both CDP and LLDP at once?
chosen: Yes, though it is somewhat redundant since they share mostly the same information.
rejected: No. Enabling LLDP automatically disables CDP, since the two use conflicting multicast addresses.

prompt: What is the default LLDP advertisement timer?
chosen: 30 seconds — half of CDP's 60.
rejected: 60 seconds, the same as CDP.

prompt: What is the default LLDP holdtime?
chosen: 120 seconds, shorter than CDP's 180.
rejected: 180 seconds, the same as CDP.

prompt: What is the LLDP reinitialisation delay?
chosen: A timer, 2 seconds by default, that makes the device wait before sending LLDP messages after LLDP activates on an interface. It gives an unstable port time to settle.
rejected: The time the device waits before rebuilding its entire LLDP neighbour table after the protocol is restarted.

prompt: Why is the reinitialisation delay useful?
chosen: If an interface is bouncing between up and down due to an unstable connection, the delay gives the port time to stabilise before LLDP starts advertising on it.
rejected: It staggers the advertisements from different interfaces so they don't all transmit at the same moment.

prompt: What command sets the LLDP reinitialisation timer?
chosen: lldp reinit, followed by the number of seconds.
rejected: lldp delay, followed by the number of seconds.

prompt: How does per-interface control differ between CDP and LLDP?
chosen: CDP uses one command, cdp enable. LLDP uses two separate commands, lldp transmit and lldp receive, so you can control sending and receiving independently.
rejected: CDP uses two commands for transmit and receive, while LLDP combines both into the single lldp enable command.

prompt: What would an interface with lldp transmit enabled but lldp receive disabled do?
chosen: It would send LLDP messages but discard any it receives.
rejected: It would receive LLDP messages and update its neighbour table but never advertise itself.

prompt: Why might you disable only LLDP transmission?
chosen: For security — you can keep receiving information about connected devices while not revealing anything about your own. It is a rare configuration though.
rejected: To reduce CPU load, since transmitting LLDP messages is far more expensive than processing received ones.

prompt: If LLDP is enabled globally, what happens on the interfaces?
chosen: Both transmission and reception are enabled on all interfaces by default. You then disable them individually if needed.
rejected: Nothing. Each interface must be enabled separately with lldp transmit and lldp receive.

prompt: What do Tx and Rx mean in show lldp interface?
chosen: Tx is transmission and Rx is reception.
rejected: Tx is the transmit queue depth and Rx is the receive queue depth.

prompt: What LLDP capability code is equivalent to CDP's S for Switch?
chosen: B, for Bridge.
rejected: S, since both protocols use the same capability codes.

prompt: What command lists LLDP neighbours?
chosen: show lldp neighbors. The LLDP commands generally mirror the CDP ones — just replace cdp with lldp.
rejected: show lldp table.

prompt: What field in show lldp neighbors detail shows the neighbour's hostname?
chosen: System Name.
rejected: Device ID, the same field name CDP uses.

prompt: What does Time remaining mean in show lldp neighbors detail?
chosen: The current holdtime — how long until the entry is removed if no further advertisements arrive.
rejected: How long the neighbour has been continuously reachable since it was first discovered.

prompt: What command shows LLDP message statistics?
chosen: show lldp traffic. It lists frames sent and received, plus errors and discards, which is useful when troubleshooting.
rejected: show lldp counters.

prompt: Given R1 shows a neighbour with Local Intrfce Gig 0/0 and Port ID Gig 0/1, how are they connected?
chosen: R1's G0/0 interface connects to the neighbour's G0/1 interface.
rejected: R1's G0/1 interface connects to the neighbour's G0/0 interface.

prompt: Can you map an entire network from CDP output on several devices?
chosen: Yes. By reading the Local Intrfce and Port ID columns on each device, you can work out every link and draw the topology.
rejected: No. CDP only shows directly connected neighbours, so you would need a routing protocol's database to see the full topology.
